entries.title: Middle East: Netanyahu says Israel rejects Trump's Gaza plan
entries.summary: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu announced Israel's rejection of US President Donald Trump's 15-point plan for Gaza. Follow DW for more.
entries.content:
Iran

Middle East: Netanyahu says Israel rejects Trump's Gaza plan

Published August 8, 2026last updated August 9, 2026

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu announced Israel's rejection of US President Donald Trump's 15-point plan for Gaza. Follow DW for more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Israel rejects Trump's Gaza plan, PM Netanyahu says

  • Houthi rebels claim attack on Saudi oil facility

  • The Revolutionary Guard says Iran will reopen the Strait of Hormuz once the US 'corrects its behavior' and accepts Iran's conditions
  • They include never threatening Iran again, lifting sanctions and releasing frozen Iranian assets
  • The Guards also say the strategic waterway's reopening does not depend on how talks with Oman develop
  • Iran says the talks are nearing their 'final' stages, with Oman calling the discussions 'positive'
  • The UAE says Iran targeted tanker transiting in Hormuz

Keep reading for the latest developments on the conflict in the Middle East on Saturday, August 8, and Sunday, August 9, 2026:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section Iran vows to release footage of Supreme Leader

Iran vows to release footage of Supreme Leader

Mizan, the Iranian judiciary's news outlet, reported that a Basij Organization deputy head promised to release footage of the Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei at a later time.

Footage of Khamenei "among the people and out in streets, as well ‌in meetings ⁠with ⁠the commanders of armed forces" will be ​released in the future, Qasem Qoraishi reportedly said.

Mojtaba Khamenei, who was appointed Supreme Leader in March, has not been seen in public since his appointment.

According to senior Iranian sources, he suffered facial disfigurement and other injuries in the strike that killed his father on February 28, the first day of US and Israeli airstrikes on Iran.

Skip next section Israel rejects Trump's Gaza plan, Netanyahu says

Israel rejects Trump's Gaza plan, Netanyahu says

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu announced that Israel has rejected US President Donald Trump's 15-point plan for Gaza.

The prime minister stressed that the Israeli military will not withdraw from Gaza until Hamas is fully disarmed.

"Israel rejects the 15-point document. The IDF (Israel's military, known as the Israel Defense Forces) will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is genuinely disarmed and will continue to thwart threats against our forces and our citizens," Netanyahu said at a Cabinet meeting.

Last month, Trump announced that his Board of Peace had reached a “historic” agreement with Hamas and other Palestinian militant groups in the Gaza Strip to disarm.

Israel designates Hamas as a terrorist group, alongside several other countries including the United States and Germany.

Skip next section Houthis attack government-controlled port of Mocha in Yemen

Houthis attack government-controlled port of Mocha in Yemen

A Yemeni government official said the Houthis attacked the crucial Red Sea port of Mocha.

Fayed al-Noman, the assistant undersecretary of the Information Ministry, said the Houthis launched missiles and drones at Mocha.

Mocha is one of the main ports under the control of Yemen's internationally recognized government backed by Saudi Arabia.

It was renovated in recent years to handle shipping that avoids the Houthi-held ports in Hodeida.

The Iran-backed Houthi rebels claimed responsibility for the attack. According to Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree, the movement’s forces carried out a “large-scale and precise” operation targeting Saudi enemy troops and weapons depots in the Mocha area.

Earlier on Sunday, the Houthis claimed responsibility for attacking the Saudi Aramco oil facility in Jizan that caused a fire.

Skip next section Iran: Talks with US won't take place while interim deal is breached

Iran: Talks with US won't take place while interim deal is breached

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said there were currently no negotiations between Iran and the United States, only an exchange of messages through intermediaries.

In remarks published by the Mehr news agency and cited by Reuters, Araghchi also said Tehran would not begin negotiations as long as Washington continued to breach the interim deal signed in June.

He reiterated Iran's stance that an agreement between Tehran and Muscat on the Strait of Hormuz was in the "final stages," though it would not reopen the strategic waterway.

Araghchi said the agreement would establish new shipping lanes to be used once the US fulfills its conditions and reopens the Strait of Hormuz to traffic.

Meanwhile, Iran's Revolutionary Guards also said they would not reopen the Strait of Hormuz until the United States accepts all of Tehran's demands.

"Our current strategy is to maintain this strait until the enemy accepts all our conditions," Guards spokesman Hossein Mohebi told state TV, according to AFP.

He added that "the strait is now actually a theatre of war for us and not just a waterway."

Skip next section Houthis say they hit refinery on Saudi Arabia's Red Sea coast

Houthis say they hit refinery on Saudi Arabia's Red Sea coast

Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels claimed responsibility on Sunday for a strike on an oil facility along Saudi Arabia's Red Sea coast.

Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the group targeted an Aramco refinery in the city of Jazan with a drone.

He added the attack was in response to Saudi drones that had breached Yemen’s airspace over the provinces of Hajjah and Saada.

Earlier on Sunday, the Saudi Energy Ministry reported a fire at a facility belonging to the Aramco refinery, adding that there were no casualties.

The ministry said the fire had been extinguished, but did not describe its cause. Aramco is Saudi Arabia's state-owned oil company.

Skip next section Welcome back to our coverage

Welcome back to our coverage

Good morning! We are reopening our blog after a nighttime break.

Stay tuned for more news and analysis on the situation in the Middle East.

Skip next section What are Iran's demands in negotiations with the US?

What are Iran's demands in negotiations with the US?

Earlier, DW reported that Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi had said talks with the United States on reopening the Strait of Hormuz depended on Washington's "compensating" Iran for the US "violation" of a June memorandum of understanding that the two nations had signed.

Aragchi and the IRGC had also pointed to "other conditions" that would need to be met.

Iran's Supreme National Security Council said the country would not lift its blockade of Hormuz until the United States "corrects its behavior."

In a statement by the council's secretary and Revolutionary Guard Commander Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr that was published on Iran's state broadcaster, said the United States must:

  • Never threaten Iran again
  • Permanently end its war against Iran and its allies in the region, namely Lebanese militants Hezbollah; Houthi rebels in Yemen; and Hamas in the Gaza Strip
  • Lift its blockade of Iranian ports and ships in the Strait of Hormuz and pull its military out of the area
  • Lift sanctions and release frozen Iranian assets 

The US has yet to respond.

Skip next section WATCH: Iran and Oman near landmark shipping agreement

WATCH: Iran and Oman near landmark shipping agreement

Iran says it is in the final stages of reaching an agreement with Oman on shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world's most strategically important waterways. Reports suggest that the deal would give Tehran oversight of vessels entering the Persian Gulf. Oman would manage outbound traffic.

If finalized, the arrangement could mark a significant shift in regional influence and raise questions about freedom of navigation, security and the balance of power in the Gulf.

DW spoke to analyst Megan Sutcliffe and former US diplomat Alan Eyre, who helped negotiate the 2015 Iran nuclear deal, about what this could mean for the region and beyond.

Skip next section Saudi-Turkey-Pakistan defense deal raises new security questions

Saudi-Turkey-Pakistan defense deal raises new security questions

On Friday, Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan unveiled a new security alliance that bears strong similarities to NATO's principles of collective defense.

The three regional powers — who are also strategic allies of the United States — have signed a defense pact that is "intended to strengthen collective deterrence against any act of aggression."

The deal is widely viewed as the three Sunni-majority nations' way of defending themselves against the rising threat from an increasingly hostile Iran, where Shiite Islam is the state religion.

The agreement could also be seen as a sign of shifting power dynamics in the region, as well as a way to hedge against an unreliable US, amid uncertainty over its long-term commitment to its role in enforcing security in the Gulf.

DW's Brent Goff spoke to experts Dania Thafer and Kamran Bokhari to learn more about what the new agreement means for the region and the US-Iran conflict.

Skip next section Oman calls Hormuz talks 'positive,' warns against attacks

Oman calls Hormuz talks 'positive,' warns against attacks

Oman's Foreign Ministry on Saturday said talks with Iran about the future of maritime traffic in the Strait of Hormuz were "proceeding in a positive and constructive atmosphere."

But Muscat warned against "repeated attacks" on cargo ships, which it said could jeopardize the negotiations, although it stopped short of explicitly naming Iran.

Tehran has been targeting ships that it claims have ties to the United States or that fail to comply with its orders.

Earlier on Saturday, Iran said talks over a deal with Oman were "approaching the final stages."

Skip next section IN DEPTH: How viable is the potential Iran-Oman Hormuz shipping deal?

IN DEPTH: How viable is the potential Iran-Oman Hormuz shipping deal?

Iran says a shipping accord with Oman is in its final stages, but analysts warn sanctions, security concerns and rival US and Iranian goals could limit its impact.

Learn more about the potential deal between Iran and Oman in this report.

Skip next section WATCH: Will Iran develop a nuclear weapon?

WATCH: Will Iran develop a nuclear weapon?

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu says he is determined to prevent what he says are Iran's plans to build nuclear weapons. But is there any evidence that Iran plans to build up its nuclear capabilities?

Skip next section UAE accuses Iran of attacking state-owned ship in Hormuz

UAE accuses Iran of attacking state-owned ship in Hormuz

The United Arab Emirates on Saturday accused Iran of attacking a tanker belonging to its state-owned Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (ADNOC) while the vessel was sailing through the Strait of Hormuz.

In a statement, the UAE's Foreign Ministry slammed what it called a "hostile" missile attack. No casualties were caused, the statement added.

The ministry also accused Iran's Revolutionary Guard (IRGC) of "acts of piracy" by attacking commercial cargo ships and using the strait to exert economic pressure on the US and its allies in the region.

The IRGC has warned it would target ships with ties to Tehran's enemies transiting the waterway or if they fail to comply with Iran's orders, such as paying a fee to pass through the Iranian naval blockade.

On Friday, ADNOC — one of the world's biggest energy producers and exporters — said Iran had attacked 15 of its ships with missiles and drones since the conflict started in late February, "including three vessels this week alone."

Iran has targeted a range of countries in the Middle East region that have ties with the US in retaliation for US and Israeli strikes.

Skip next section Iran says US must agree to its terms before it reopens Hormuz

Iran says US must agree to its terms before it reopens Hormuz

The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said Saturday that Iran will reopen the Strait of Hormuz after the United States agrees to its terms.

On Friday, an American official said progress in talks between Iran and Oman could lead to the reopening of the strait. Hormuz has been largely closed to maritime traffic for months as Iran and the US each impose their own blockades.

While Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi on Saturday said talks with Oman were nearing their "final stages," he warned that progress was "not a sign" that the strait's reopening was imminent.

"The reopening of the Strait of Hormuz is subject to other conditions and compensation for the violation of the memorandum of understanding by the United States," Araghchi said, referring to a June agreement between Washington and Tehran.

On Saturday, Iran's Tasnim news agency, which is affiliated with the IRGC, reported that Guards spokesman Hossein Mohebbi said that Hormuz's reopening "is subject ​to the specific mechanisms ​and conditions of the ​Islamic Republic of Iran ‌and is not related to ​the ⁠negotiations between Iran and Oman."

"The enemy is forced to accept Iran's conditions for the opening of the strait and to refrain from the interference that it is currently making in the negotiations — which have almost reached their end — between Iran, Oman and other countries," Mohebbi said.

Traffic through the strait, which was the conduit for 20% of the world's oil and gas before the war, has been severely restricted since the war began five months ago.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has said that Iran will reopen the Strait of Hormuz on the condition that the United States accepts its terms in full.

The Guards have also said ongoing talks with Oman, its neighbor across the strait, would not have any bearing on whether Tehran lifts its blockade of Hormuz.

The UAE said Saturday that one of its tankers was targeted while trying to sail through the strait.

We will bring you more on these stories and more on the war between the US and Iran and the rest of the region.

entries.title: Ukraine and Russia exchange attacks as Kyiv buys new ATACMS
entries.summary: Overnight drone and missile attacks killed several and injured dozens more in both Ukraine and Russia. As Kyiv seeks to defend itself it has now reportedly finalized a deal to buy US missile systems from Turkey.
entries.content:
Europe

Ukraine and Russia exchange attacks as Kyiv buys new ATACMS

August 9, 2026

Overnight drone and missile attacks killed several and injured dozens more in both Ukraine and Russia. As Kyiv seeks to defend itself it has now reportedly finalized a deal to buy US missile systems from Turkey.

Overnight drone and missile attacks have killed several people and injured dozens more according to various local authorities in Ukraine and Russia.

In the southern Russian city of Belgorod, near the Ukrainian border, at least five people were killed and 25 injured.

Belgorod's acting governor said that several apartment blocks had been hit overnight and images posted to social media showed several fires.

Belgorod is a key logistics hub for Russian offensives in Kharkiv and the Donbass.

Russian authorities, who said more than 150 Ukrainian drones had been downed by their forces overnight, also reported attacks on the Black Sea ports of Novorossiysk and Gelendzhik.

Novorossiysk is home to key Russian oil export facilities.

'Russia continuing its war on global food security' says Zelenskyy

Russian attacks targeted oil refineries in the Sumy region as well as the port city of Odesa, where President Voldymyr Zelenskyy said at least eight people had been injured.

The Odesa strikes targeted oil facilities in the southern port.

Odesa is also one of Ukraine's most important agricultural export hubs.

Zelenskyy said that with Sunday's attack, "Russia is continuing its war on global food security."

Two people were also killed and at least 21 injured in a Russian attack on Kharkiv in eastern Ukraine, according to regional head Oleh Syniehubov.

Across the border, Russia claimed its forces had taken control of two villages in eastern Donetsk, though the claim could not be independently verified.

Kyiv arming itself against 4-year Russia invasion

As Russia's war on Ukraine drags on toward the five-year mark, Kyiv is again short on defensive weapons.

Kyiv has desperately sought to acquire more medium and long-range weapons systems from the US with mixed results.

Now, Ukraine is turning to Turkey for help as the US reportedly depletes its own stockpiles with its still unresolved war in Iran.

On Sunday, Ukraine's military news outlet Militarnyi reported that it would be purchasing 70 ATACMS and 12 M270 multiple-launch rocket systems from Turkey in an order that will also include more than 2,500 227mm rockets with cluster-munitions payloads.

The US, which has 30 days to approve the sale, estimates its total value at $283 million (€245 million).

The ATACMS in question are of an older design, with a range limited to 165 kilometers (102.5 miles).

Edited by: Rana Taha

entries.title: Study: Obesity 'bigger cancer risk' than previously thought
entries.summary: A new study has found that being significantly overweight could be responsible for more cases of cancer than previously known. Abdominal fat, in particular, increases the risk of cancer — especially among women.
entries.content:
August 9, 2026

A new study has found that being significantly overweight could be responsible for more cases of cancer than previously known. Abdominal fat, in particular, increases the risk of cancer — especially among women.

Being overweight or obese significantly increases the risk of developing colon cancer, breast cancer or liver cancer, and is a major risk factor for 10 other types of cancer, a new study has found.

Until recently, researchers believed that 2% to 8% of all cancer cases were attributable to excess body weight. But a new study by a team led by Hermann Brenner, an epidemiologist with the German Cancer Research Center  (DKFZ), suggests that this was a serious underestimate.

According to the study, up to 11.5% of cancers may be attributable to being overweight.

The DKFZ researchers "have not only updated existing risk estimates, but have also questioned whether the link between excess weight and cancer may have been underestimated until now," Michael Leitzmann, an epidemiologist at the University of Regensburg, told DW.

Leitzmann, who was not involved in the study, researches diet, body weight, physical activity and the development of chronic diseases at the university's Institute of Epidemiology and Prevention, and has advised German Cancer Aid.

The abdominal-fat 'trigger'

The DKFZ team changed its research methods for the new study. Previous research used body mass index (BMI), which is calculated based on height and weight, as an indicator of excess weight. But BMI does not distinguish between fat and muscle mass, and does not provide information on how fat is distributed throughout the body.

This is important, because not all fat is the same. Fat cells that accumulate around the abdomen are more than just a passive store for excess calories, unlike those in other parts of the body. "They trigger what is known as a chronic inflammatory metabolic state," Leitzmann said.

Excess abdominal fat functions like a gland that releases various signaling molecules, known as adipokines. These travel through the bloodstream to different parts of the body, where they influence other metabolic processes — including cell growth and division, as well as the inhibition of programmed cell death. "These are all mechanisms that can contribute to the development and subsequent growth of tumors," Leitzmann said.

The DKFZ researchers therefore focused not only on BMI but also on waist circumference and the waist-to-hip ratio. Data from 458,543 women and men from the UK Biobank, which holds one of the world's biggest health datasets, were included in the study. The participants were followed for and average of 12 years, during which 50,000 new cases of cancer were identified.

Understanding previous underestimates

The researchers wanted to rule out a potential methodological bias in previous studies: the fact that cancer can lead to weight loss even before diagnosis — that is, while it is still developing.

That suggests that previous studies failed to identify a link between obesity and cancer because the participants had already lost weight because they had developed cancer by the time they entered the study.

For this reason, the team excluded the first few years following the participants' enrollment from the analysis. Only cancer cases that occurred seven years after the start of the observation period were considered — and that made the statistical link between being overweight and cancer clearer.

Women at risk

The study suggests that the proportion of overweight women who develop cancer is higher than that of men, but Leitzmann urges caution when interpreting these findings. Further studies with a similar design are needed to see whether the results can be replicated.

Leitzmann offered a theory on why being overweight might have a more severe impact on women. Being overweight is blamed, among other things, for breast, uterine and ovarian cancers. "These types of cancer, which affect women, are hormone-dependent," Leitzmann said. For example, the hormone estrogen can stimulate the growth of breast cancer, and excess abdominal fat can contribute to elevated estrogen levels.

Most people are now aware that obesity increases the risk of cardiovascular disease or Type 2 diabetes, Leitzmann said. Conversely, this also means that people who lose weight also reduce their risk of heart attacks, strokes and diabetes.

Though the DKFZ study emphasizes the increased risk associated with obesity, Leitzmann said the findings were also a reason for optimism: "To me, this clearly indicates that, by preventing obesity, we will be able to make a greater contribution to cancer prevention than previously assumed."

This article was originally written in German.

entries.title: Indonesia: Mount Bromo wildfire grows, spurs park closure
entries.summary: Indonesian authorities have closed a popular national park until further notice. Strong winds and rough terrain are making it difficult for firefighters to extinguish the blaze.
entries.content:
August 9, 2026

Indonesian authorities have closed a popular national park until further notice. Strong winds and rough terrain are making it difficult for firefighters to extinguish the blaze.

Authorities in Indonesia closed the Bromo Tengger Semeru National Park in East Java until further notice on Saturday due to a wildfire that has scorched some 176 hectares (435 acres) of land on Mount Bromo since it began on Monday.

The blaze, one of several currently burning across Indonesia, has mobilized hundreds of firefighters, park rangers, police, soldiers and volunteers at one of Indonesia's most popular tourist destinations.

What do we know about the wildfires situation in Indonesia?

Helicopters and drones are in use in the air and firebreaks are being created by crews on the ground.

Officials describe the situation as challenging, pointing to high winds and rough terrain, with many areas difficult to access on steep volcanic slopes.

"These conditions make air operations important to reach areas that cannot be accessed optimally by land," one official said.

Dry conditions and winds are fueling the spread of the flames according to Indonesia's Meteorological, Climatological and Geophysical Agency.

Authorities say the fire was sparked during land clearing work.

Though fires — often illegally started by plantation owners and farmers to clear for planting — are common in the region, the current El Nino weather pattern and seasonal dry winds from Australia have combined to make this year especially prone to wildfire and drought.

Indonesia has lost more than 107,000 hectares of land to fire in the first half of 2026, over twice the area destroyed in wildfires in 2023, when the last El-Nino pattern started.

Edited by: Rana Taha

entries.title: India: Ex-Education Minister Pradhan says Gen Z 'misled'
entries.summary: Dharmendra Pradhan spoke for the first time since his resignation as education minister following mass protests against him. He said he "suffered" because of Gen Z, who led the protests. Follow DW for more.
entries.content:
Asia

India: Ex-Education Minister Pradhan says Gen Z 'misled'

Published August 9, 2026last updated August 9, 2026

Dharmendra Pradhan spoke for the first time since his resignation as education minister following mass protests against him. He said he "suffered" because of Gen Z, who led the protests. Follow DW for more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Former Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan says he had offered to step down amid protests against him
  • 'Some people misled Gen Z' during the protests, Pradhan has alleged

Here's a roundup of the biggest headlines from India on Sunday, August 9: 

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click hereto add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section JD Vance calls Modi to boost ties between India and US

JD Vance calls Modi to boost ties between India and US

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi said he received a call from US Vice President JD Vanceto discuss boosting Indo-US relations on trade, defense, emerging technologies, energy security and critical minerals.

The two leaders reviewed progress in the India-US Comprehensive Global Strategic Partnership, a government statement said.

Skip next section Instant payments will remain free for users, government clarifies

Instant payments will remain free for users, government clarifies

The Indian government has clarified that its real-time payment service, called Unified Payments Interface (UPI), will remain free-of-charge for consumers. It said only merchants will have to pay a "nominal" charge for some transactions.

The clarification came after the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007 was passed in Lok Sabha earlier this week. The bill caused much concern over a potential charge on UPI transactions.

Earlier reports had suggested that the bill would allow the government to permit banks and payment companies to charge fees on UPI and other digital payments in the future.

Addressing the concern, the Ministry of Finance clarified that all person-to-person transactions will remain free of charge.

It however said that a limited set of merchant transactions will incur transaction charges when the MDR (Merchant Discount Rate) charges are introduced.

MDR is a fee levied on merchants by banks to help meet costs related to processing of transactions, settlement and infrastructure.

Since its introduction by the Reserve Bank of India in 2016, UPI has become one of the most popular payment methods across the country.

In 2025 alone, the UPI transaction load stood at 228.5 billion transactions in India. The total value of UPI transactions reached Rs 299.74 trillion (€2.7 trillion, $3.4 trillion).

Skip next section Gen Z was 'misled,' says Dharmendra Pradhan

Gen Z was 'misled,' says Dharmendra Pradhan

Former Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan broke his silence for the first time since he resigned following massive youth protests.

Speaking at a ceremony on Saturday, Pradhan said: "Gen Z is our children. Some people attempted to mislead them."

Pradhan's  acknowledgment of the protests and his resignation came some 15 days after he quit as the education minister.

Pradhan said he "suffered" because of Gen Z's stubbornness but had come to realize that the new generation must be understood rather than resisted.

Speaking about his resignation, Pradhan said he had approached Prime Minister Narendra Modi and offered to resign from the Union Council of Ministers.

"The post was not important to me," Pradhan told a gathering at an event at GM University in Bhubaneswar, according to Indian news agency Press Trust of India.

Pradhan's resignation was the biggest demand made by the young protesters, led by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP).

The protests were triggered over exam irregularities in competitive exams, especially the NEET exam, which is a key requirement for those wishing to enter medical schools across India.

Reportedly, at least 21 students had taken their own lives after the NEET exam was cancelled because of a question paper leak. It was then held at a later date.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Hello! This is Midhat from the New Delhi bureau bringing you all the latest updates from across India.

Dharmendra Pradhan, who resigned under public pressure after massive youth protests, has broken his silence. He alleged that Gen Z, who was leading the protest movement against him, was misled during the protests over exam irregularities.

Meanwhile, after much confusion and debate over a potential fee on apps-based instant digital payments, the Indian government has clarified that consumers will not have to pay charges for such payments and only merchants will have to pay a "nominal" fee.

On the international front, US Vice President JD Vance called up Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi to discuss strengthening cooperation between India and the US on trade, defense and energy security.

Stay tuned as we bring you more from India.

entries.title: Australia: Jetstar, Qatar Airways planes almost collide on Sydney Airport tarmac
entries.summary: A flight crew member was injured in a near-miss collision on the runway at Australia's Sydney Airport. An investigation has been launched to determine what caused the incident.
entries.content:
Australia

Australia: 2 planes almost collide on Sydney Airport tarmac

August 9, 2026

A flight crew member was injured in a near-miss collision on the runway at Australia's Sydney Airport. An investigation has been launched to determine what caused the incident.

Two passenger aircraft —  a Jetstar and a Qatar Airways plane —  came close to crashing into each other on the tarmac at Australia's  busiest Sydney Airport on Sunday.

A crew member was injured and the incident has triggered a probe by the country's safety regulators.

What do we know about the near-miss collision?

The Jetstar A320 was taxiing for takeoff to the Gold Coast in the state of Queensland when its flight crew saw the Qatar Airways Boeing 777 —  which was being towed by an aircraft tug —  in close proximity on a crossing taxiway, the Australian Transport Safety Bureau (ATSB) said in a statement.

"Both aircraft were stopped abruptly", the statement said, leading to a Jestar cabin crew member moving through the cabin being injured and the connection between the 777 nose gear and aircraft tug suffering damage.

The injured crew member was treated by paramedics.

How are Australian authorities handling the incident?

The ATSB said that investigators were gathering data from both the planes, air traffic control, and interviewing crew and tug operators to determine the cause of the near collision.

The regulator put out a call for witnesses at the airport to send in any visuals of the incident.

Jetstar — which is a low-cost subsidiary of Australia's national carrier Qantas — said it was also conducting its own investigation.

"Our aircraft was following ⁠instructions ​by Air Traffic Control when the ​pilots were forced to brake firmly after another aircraft came in ​close proximity," a ‌Jetstar spokesperson said.

There was no immediate statement from Qatar Airways, which is the flag carrier of Qatar.

Meanwhile, flights at Sydney Airport were experiencing delays following the incident, government agency Airservices Australia said.

Sunday's incident ⁠comes a day after Sydney Airport witnessed widespread delays ⁠sparked by Airservices Australia authorizing "departure spacing" due to roster issues with air traffic controllers.

Edited by: Rana Taha

entries.title: Germany news: German kidnapped in Niger released — Algeria
entries.summary: Algeria says a German citizen has been released after a "criminal armed group" kidnapped him in Niger for two weeks. Meanwhile, Germany is moving to counter the threats posed by drones. Follow DW.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: German kidnapped in Niger released — Algeria

Published August 8, 2026last updated August 9, 2026

Algeria says a German citizen has been released after a "criminal armed group" kidnapped him in Niger for two weeks. Meanwhile, Germany is moving to counter the threats posed by drones. Follow DW.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Algeria says it has taken charge of a German citizen kidnapped in Niger some two weeks ago
  • Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt says Germany is to expand drone security research
  • Low water levels in the Rhine and other rivers are posing a growing risk for Germany, an expert says
  • Protesters in eastern Germany have called for new elections, while demonstrators in Berlin have demanded a ban on far-right parties

Here is a roundup of the stories from and about Germany that are hitting the headlines on the weekend of August 8-9, 2026:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section Berlin police investigating shooting incidents amid rise in gun crime

Berlin police investigating shooting incidents amid rise in gun crime

Berlin police are looking into two incidents in which shots were fired, as shooting incidents in the German capital seem on the rise.

In one incident early on Sunday, shots were fired at a hairdressing salon in the Marzahn-Hellersdorf district in the city's northeast, while a gunshot hole was also found at a nearby nightclub, a police spokeswoman said.

She said no one was injured.

That was, however, not the case with another shooting incident in Kreuzberg on Friday evening.

There, a 22-year-old man was shot and injured by an assailant, who fled the scene.

Homicide squad officers are investigating possible links to previous shooting incidents in the area.

Last year, Berlin police set up the Ferrum specialist unit to investigate gun crime.

Skip next section German national kidnapped in Niger freed — Algeria

German national kidnapped in Niger freed — Algeria

Algeria said on Saturday that a German citizen kidnapped by an armed criminal group some two weeks ago in neighboring Niger was safe and in the hands of the Algerian military. 

The German national was taken in charge by the Algerian army's security services on Friday, according to a statement from the Defense Ministry shared on the official Algerian news agency.

He has now been taken on a special flight from Guezzam in the far south to the Boufarik military base near the capital Algiers, it said, adding that he was in "good health" and would be handed to German authorities "at a later date."

No details were provided on how the German national was freed.

A spokesperson for Germany's Foreign Office confirmed to the German DPA news agency that the federal government was aware of the case.

Niger, which has been under military rule since a July 2023 coup, has in the past few years been wracked by violence from jihadis linked to the al-Qaeda or the "Islamic State" (IS) terrorist groups.

Skip next section Trucks underway in several states as Sunday motorway ban lifted

Trucks underway in several states as Sunday motorway ban lifted

Several states have lifted a rule banning most trucks from using motorways on Sundays and public holidays in view of the low river water levels currently hampering cargo vessels.

The DPA news agency reported that a number of trucks have already been sighted on motorways in the western state of North Rhine-Westphalia (NRW).

The NRW transport minister, Oliver Krischer, said that "this exceptional regulation allows us to ensure that delivery chains are maintained and supply shortages are avoided."

Industrial associations have welcomed the lifting of the truck ban.

But one of Germany's main unions, Verdi, has criticized the move.

"This measure comes at the cost of employees in the transport and logistics branch and calls into question the legal protection of Sundays and public holidays as days of rest and recreation," said Uwe Köpke, who heads the union's postal services, freight forwarding and logistics department.

Lower Saxony, Rhineland-Palatinate and Saarland are so far the only other states to have lifted the ban as one of the measures announced by Transport Minister Steffen Bilger last week to mitigate the economic effect of the cargo shipping shortfalls.

In NRW and Lower Saxony, the suspension of the ban is to run initially until August 31, and in Rhineland-Palatinate and Saarland until September 30 at the latest.

In NRW, all trucks will also be able to use the motorways on Saturdays during the day in the current summer holidays as an exemption to an existing regulation.

Skip next section Germany's trade deficit with China grows in first half of 2026

Germany's trade deficit with China grows in first half of 2026

New preliminary data released on Sunday has shown that German exports to China fell more than 12% year-on-year from January through June. German imports from China rose 8.9%.

That raises the trade deficit to about €55 billion ($63.6 billion) from €40 billion for the same period in 2025.

The data from the state-run agency Germany Trade & Invest (GTAI) reflects the decreasing reliance by Chinese firms on European imports.

They show that although China remains Germany's top trading partner, the Asian powerhouse is now only the ninth-biggest market for German goods, with far smaller economies like Austria and Switzerland buying more from Germany in 2026.

As recently as 2021, China was Germany's second-biggest ​export market.

The US remains Germany's single-biggest foreign market, despite a drop in German exports there amid protectionist tariffs introduced under President Donald Trump.

Skip next section Rheinmetall's Papperger says he's not 'chickening out' amid threats

Rheinmetall's Papperger says he's not 'chickening out' amid threats

The CEO of arms giant Rheinmetall, Armin Papperger, has said he will not be intimidated despite the many threats that have been made to his safety.

"These jobs must be done, and anyone that can't take the pressure doesn't belong in this job," he told the DPA news agency, saying "chickening out" was no option in his field.

Pappberger, 63, who is believed to be a possible target of Russian murder plots, is under constant police protection at a level similar to that given to Chancellor Friedrich Merz.

Rheinmetall is supplying large quantities of weapons to Ukraine amid the Russian invasion, potentially putting the company in Moscow's crosshairs.  

Germany's domestic intelligence services recently called on employees in the defense sector to be very vigilant amid the threat of espionage and sabotage by Russian state agencies.

Skip next section Dobrindt announces stepped-up drone security research

Dobrindt announces stepped-up drone security research

Germany is establishing a new drone security research facility as it seeks to counter a growing threat from UAVs that are possibly under foreign control, Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt has told Sunday's edition of the Bild tabloid.

"The arms race in drone technology requires dedicated research units to keep pace," he said.

He said the new center, to be established on August 18 at a German Aerospace Center (DLR) test airport in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, would develop and test technologies to protect against drones.

His remarks come after a number of incidents involving drones in the past week raised security concerns.

You can read more on Dobrindt's statements on security here.

Skip next section Welcome back

Welcome back

The DW newsroom in Bonn says a warm guten Morgen to its readers as we resume our coverage of all things German on Sunday.

Concerns about national security amid a myriad of threats are featuring largely in today's headlines, with, for example, the interior minister warning of hybrid warfare after several drone incidents.

Some of those threats even target particular people, as the CEO of arms giant Rheinmetall, Armin Papperger, is experiencing.

And nature itself is also posing a security challenge, with the lack of water in the Rhine and other rivers having a widening impact on the economy and beyond.

Read on for more on these and other stories.

Skip next section We are pausing our coverage

We are pausing our coverage

We are pausing our coverage as the clock is about to strike midnight here in Bonn. Join us again on Sunday, when we will update this blog with the latest news from Germany.

Skip next section WATCH: CDU's Saxony-Anhalt candidate warns against AfD taking power

WATCH: CDU's Saxony-Anhalt candidate warns against AfD taking power

Sven Schulze, state premier and the CDU's candidate in the upcoming regional election in Saxony-Anhalt has slammed the AfD for its xenophobia, and underscored his state's reliance on exports and foreign workers.

Skip next section WATCH: Why low Rhine water levels are a growing risk for Germany

WATCH: Why low Rhine water levels are a growing risk for Germany

Germany's most important river is running low unusually early in the year.

Ships are still moving on the Rhine, but falling water levels are forcing many to carry lighter loads. Professor Kerstin Stahl, a hydrologist at the University of Freiburg, explains what is driving the drought and why the consequences reach far beyond shipping.

Skip next section Thousands call for Merz resignation, new elections at protest in eastern Germany

Thousands call for Merz resignation, new elections at protest in eastern Germany

Some 10,000 people protested in the eastern German city of Plauen to call for Chancellor Friedrich Merz's resignation and for new elections to be held immediately.

While the "Unity for Germany" protest was officially independent of political parties, a local pro-democracy group warned that some of the rally's organizers are right-wing extremists.

"The event is being promoted by relevant far-right channels; on Facebook, the comments on the demonstration contain hateful remarks, and the calls to action spread antisemitic and ethno-nationalist narratives," the Alliance for Democracy, Tolerance and Civil Courage said.

Apart from the government's resignation and new elections, the protesters' 11 demands also include:

  • The immediate deportation of 'all convicted, criminal and illegal migrants'

  • Lower energy prices

  • A

    cheaper nationwide monthly travel pass, for €29 ($33.50)

  • Reform to public service broadcasting

  • Scrapping the carbon dioxide tax

  • Introducing a direct democracy model like in Switzerland

  • Reducing bureaucracy

The protesters also chanted "We are the people," the slogan that was used at pro-democracy rallies during the peaceful revolution of 1989 in East Germany that preceded the end of the former German Democratic Republic.

Many German national flags, as well as banners of the historical Kingdom of Saxony — often used by the far-right Free Saxons party — were seen at the rally, as were blue peace flags with white doves, the German news agency dpa reported.

Skip next section Demonstrations in Germany call for ban on far-right parties

Demonstrations in Germany call for ban on far-right parties

Around 800 people demonstrated in Berlin, calling for the Federal Constitutional Court to review political parties suspected of right-wing extremism.

Eleven such demonstrations were planned across Germany on Saturday. The "Prüf," which translates to "check" or "examine," initiative, founded by activist Nico Semsrott, is behind the rallies.

Citing a legal opinion published in late June by the Society for Civil Rights that declared the Alternative for Germany (AfD) party unconstitutional, speakers called for a corresponding review by the Federal Constitutional Court in Karlsruhe.

Many of the demonstrators' posters bore the slogan, "Examine today — protect tomorrow."

However, the Bundestag, the Bundesrat, or the federal government must file a motion to ban the party in order to initiate such a review.

In early May 2025, the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution classified the AfD as a "confirmed far-right extremist movement," but suspended the designation after a legal challenge.

In February, a Cologne court said the agency can’t use the designation while the court evaluates the party’s lawsuit.

The AfD vehemently rejects accusations of extremism.

Skip next section German tour bus overturns in Norway, injuring several passengers

German tour bus overturns in Norway, injuring several passengers

Several people were injured after a German tour bus overturned in Norway, Norwegian public broadcaster NRK reported, citing police sources.

According to the report, some 34 German tourists were on board.

Several passengers sustained minor injuries in the incident, while four were taken to hospital.

The bus was traveling to the Trondelag region of central Norway.

The bus reportedly overturned on a bend of the E6 highway and ended up lying on its side in the grass beside the road.

The cause of the accident was initially unclear.

According to NRK, no other vehicle was involved.

Skip next section European team ends 100-day 'Mars' sojourn in Cologne

European team ends 100-day 'Mars' sojourn in Cologne

Six men and women from six different countries on Friday ended their 100-day stay in cramped, artificially lit isolation as part of a study to prepare future space missions to the moon, Mars and beyond.

The participants, from Germany, France, Italy, the Netherlands, Poland and Portugal, are now able to return to their daily lives — following a recovery phase — after leaving the simulation facility at the German Aerospace Centre (DLR) in the western city of Cologne.

The goal of the SOLIS100 study was conducted on behalf of the European Space Agency (ESA) and aimed to investigate the effects of long-duration space missions  on health and performance.

The participants had to live from non-perishable foodstuffs and were not allowed personal contact with family or friends.

 

 Every day, they carried out scientific work, medical data collection, a strict exercise program and station maintenance.  

Skip next section Culture Minister Weimer calls for Infantino's resignation

Culture Minister Weimer calls for Infantino's resignation

Wolfram Weimer, the commissioner for culture and media, has become the first member of the federal government to call for FIFA President Gianni Infantino to step down.

"Infantino has seriously damaged world football with his planned sell-off of the World Cup," he told the German DPA news agency on Saturday.

"He has lost the trust of the European football community and should not stand for re-election next year," he said.

Weimer called on the German Football Federation (DFB) to show "active resistance" against Infantino.

"With its 24,000 clubs and eight million members, the DFB is the largest sports federation in the world (by individual registered members). Its voice carries weight," he said.

Infantino has faced a storm of criticism since he unveiled plans last week to sell World Cup rights to private investors for billions.

He withdrew the proposal after major protests, including a threat by UEFA to boycott the World Cup.

entries.title: Canada: British Columbia declares emergency as fires spread
entries.summary: More than 20,000 people have been forced from their homes by out-of-control wildfires in Canada's British Columbia, where 105 blazes are currently burning.
entries.content:
Canada

Canada: British Columbia declares emergency as fires spread

August 9, 2026

More than 20,000 people have been forced from their homes by out-of-control wildfires in Canada's British Columbia, where 105 blazes are currently burning.

Canadian officials on Saturday declared a state of emergency in British Columbia after more than 20,000 people were ordered to flee a fast-moving wildfire.

Describing the intensity of the blaze, British Columbia Premier David Eby said a fire official compared it to "a bomb going off."

"He described flames on a 100-foot (30-meter) tree, flames going 200 feet above that, and the fire creating its own weather system, which creates lightning," Eby said.

"Homes have been lost, and properties have been destroyed. Some people became trapped as conditions changed very quickly, and needed to be rescued," he added.

Wildfire in British Columbia nearly doubles in size overnight

The fire, first reported Friday evening, grew rapidly overnight, triggering widespread evacuation orders.

By Saturday, it had spread to about 9,500 hectares (23,500 acres), prompting all 12,000 residents of the Summerland district to evacuate.

The Summerland blaze is one of many fires challenging emergency crews across British Columbia.

The province has seen 70 new wildfires over the past week, and 105 are currently burning, according to British Columbia Minister of Forests Ravi Parmar.

Canada grapples with large wildfires

Fires have scorched 4 million hectares in Canada in 2026, according to the Canadian Interagency Forest Fire Center.

Blazes flared up in several regions, including Ontario and Quebec, this year as hot, dry conditions fueled fires in dense forest areas.

In recent years, Canada has faced a growing number of destructive wildfire seasons. 

Edited by: Louis Oelofse

entries.title: FIFA warns against 'concerted effort' to undermine Gianni Infantino
entries.summary: Pressure is mounting on the FIFA president Gianni Infantino after plans to sell a stake in the World Cup collapsed and fresh allegations emerged relating to his time at UEFA.
entries.content:
Switzerland

FIFA warns against 'concerted effort' to undermine Infantino

August 9, 2026

Pressure is mounting on the FIFA president Gianni Infantino after plans to sell a stake in the World Cup collapsed and fresh allegations emerged relating to his time at UEFA.

FIFA warned against what it calls a "concerted and ongoing effort" to "undermine" the organization and its president, Gianni Infantino.

The statement, issued late on Saturday, comes amid a growing dispute over Infantino's leadership after the failed plan to create a subsidiary to run the men's World Cup and other events, with up to a 20% stake offered to external investors.

The proposal drew criticism from European governing body UEFA, which threatened to boycott future World Cups, as well as several national associations and senior FIFA officials, and prompted calls for Infantino to resign.

Amid the growing criticism Infantino persuaded FIFA's Board of Management to express its full support for him at a crisis meeting in Rabat, Morocco, on Wednesday. 

Report raises new questions over Infantino

The pressure on Infantino intensified on Friday when British newspaper the Daily Telegraph reported a six-figure sum was paid to a female employee alleged to have been in a relationship with him during his time as UEFA general secretary.

UEFA confirmed a departure payment and said it also funded her MBA course, stating both were in line with regulations at the time.

A FIFA spokesman told the Telegraph on Friday: "FIFA president Gianni Infantino strongly denies these allegations, and they are categorically untrue."

Responding to the latest scrutiny, FIFA said on Saturday, without directly mentioning the Telegraph report, "recent reporting has included unsubstantiated assertions and demonstrably false claims concerning FIFA and its President."

Investment plan dispute deepens leadership crisis

The fallout over the shelved private investment plan has overshadowed Infantino's bid for a fourth term as FIFA president.

After this week's crisis meeting, UEFA said it no longer has confidence in him, and Norwegian FA President Lise Klaveness called for his resignation.

Despite the controversy, Infantino retains strong backing among FIFA members, with the Confederation of African Football (CAF) unanimously supporting his leadership and South American governing body CONMEBOL opposing any attempt to remove him without a vote of all member associations.

FIFA said that those who lacked the support of its member associations should not seek to achieve "allegation, insinuation or misinformation what they cannot achieve through FIFA's established democratic processes."

Edited by: Emmy Sasipornkarn

entries.title: Germany: Interior Minister warns of 'daily' hybrid warfare
entries.summary: German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt says attacks by foreign powers have become a constant threat to Germany. His remarks come just days after an explosive-laden drone was found at Leipzig airport.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany: Interior Minister warns of 'daily' hybrid warfare

August 9, 2026

German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt says attacks by foreign powers have become a constant threat to Germany. His remarks come just days after an explosive-laden drone was found at Leipzig airport.

Germany's Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt on Sunday warned that hybrid warfare attacks had become a daily threat to the country.

"We're not at war, but we are the daily target of hybrid warfare," Dobrindt told the newspaper Bild am Sonntag following the discovery of a drone carrying explosives at Leipzig/Halle Airport.

"Espionage, sabotage, cyberattacks, or covert operations by foreign powers aimed at destabilizing Germany or inflicting direct harm are a constant reality," Dobrindt said.

He also noted that the country is stepping up research into drones to address new security threats.

A new drone security research center will be established later in August at a German Aerospace Center (DLR) test airport in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, Dobrindt said. 

Drones spotted above military base in west Germany

On Saturday, Germany's armed forces confirmed that two drones had been spotted late on Thursday over a German military base in Mechernich in the western state of North Rhine-Westphalia near the Belgian border.

The drones were detected at around 10 p.m. (2000 GMT) over the Bundeswehr base, a German armed forces spokesperson said.

German media reported that the base hosts personnel responsible for the maintenance of US Patriot air defense systems, which play a key role in defending Ukraine against Russian aerial attacks.

Drone incident at Leipzig airport

The sighting in Mechernich comes just two days after the discovery of a drone carrying explosives a Ukrainian transport plane at Leipzig/Halle Airport, an incident Dobrindt called a "hybrid attack scenario."

While German government officials have refrained from publicly blaming any foreign country over the Leipzig incident, some lawmakers have pointed fingers at Russia, which has been at war with Ukraine since ​its full-scale invasion of the country in 2022.

On Friday, the Russian Embassy in Berlin dismissed the Leipzig event as a "fabricated provocation" and said Russia was once more being accused of hostile actions "without the slightest evidence being presented."

Edited by: Louis Oelofse
